entries.title: Roy Cooper Flips a Key Senate Seat in North Carolina
entries.summary: The Democrat’s win in a battleground state is a major pickup for his party.
entries.content:
Democrat Roy Cooper is projected to win North Carolina’s open Senate seat in his race against Republican Michael Whatley.

Perhaps the most surprising element of the race was the lack of surprise in the ordinarily competitive state. Cooper, a popular former governor, pulled away from Whatley in polling and fundraising. As a result, national GOP attention shifted toward defending incumbents in states like Kansas and South Carolina.

Cooper’s win marks the first time a Democrat has won a North Carolina Senate seat since Kay Hagan’s 2008 victory, which was also the last time the state voted for a Democrat for president. Cooper will replace outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis, who publicly broke with Trump after deciding not to run for reelection. As elections become increasingly nationalized, North Carolina will become one of only a handful of states with one Democratic and one Republican senator.

Whatley was seeking elected office for the first time. He previously served as chair of the North Carolina Republican Party but is best known for his time as chair of the Republican National Committee. President Donald Trump and his allies aggressively pushed Whatley to run for the open Senate seat.

“I have a mission for my friends in North Carolina, and that is to get Michael Whatley to run for the U.S. Senate,” Trump posted on Truth Social days before Whatley formally joined the race. “HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

Tillis endorsed Whatley but recently told Politico that “we needed probably a more moderate type of profile.”
APTOPIX Election 2026 North Carolina (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)Whatley spent his campaign touting Trump’s support. In the final months of the campaign, other Republican candidates grew more comfortable breaking with the president on immigration, the Iran war and the economy. Whatley, though, stuck close to Trump.

The situation looked so grim for Whatley that his campaign paused its airing of TV ads for two weeks in October.

Mid-October FEC filings show the Republican candidate raised just $13.7 million during the two-year election cycle, while Cooper raised nearly that much money in just the three-month period from July to September — and $47.2 million overall for the cycle.

That ultimately eased the path for Cooper, who ran an affordability-focused agenda and traveled the state on a “Make stuff cost less” tour. Cooper most recently served two terms as governor after a decades-long career in state electoral politics.

Cooper previously outperformed Democrats at the top of the ticket, winning gubernatorial elections in 2016 and 2020 even as the state voted for Trump in both elections.

As governor, Cooper set a record for the most vetoes in the state as he battled with the Republican-controlled state legislature. He focused on Medicaid expansion and public school funding, and he’s likely to deliver a reliable party-line vote for Democrats.
entries.author: Chase Pellegrini de Paur

entries.title: Democrat Chris Pappas Wins Election to U.S. Senate From New Hampshire
entries.summary: The race was one of a handful that will help determine which party controls the Senate.
entries.content:
By Holly Ramer

CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire on Tuesday, keeping a critical open U.S. Senate seat under Democratic control.

The race to fill the seat being vacated by three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen was one of a handful that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans were hoping to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress while Democrats sought to hold the seat as part of their effort to win control of the chamber.

While outsiders were on the ballot elsewhere, the race for the seat being vacated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen featured two candidates who tried to tap into anti-establishment angst from the inside. Sununu railed against “career politicians” despite having spent three terms in the U.S. House and one in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008. Pappas told voters “Our country is ready for change” while seeking to remain in Washington, where he has represented the state’s 1st Congressional District since 2019.

New Hampshire voters haven’t elected a Republican to Congress since 2010. They also have voted for Democrats for president since 2004, though Republicans have dominated at the state level in recent years. With the win, Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator.

Pappas, 46, grew up working in his family’s Manchester restaurant, which opened in 1917 and claims to have invented chicken tenders. After college, he served as a state lawmaker, county treasurer and state executive councilor before being elected to Congress. In September, he defeated a democratic socialist and other opponents by a wide margin to win the Democratic primary.

“This is a time for a new generation of leadership in the United States Senate who understands the problems New Hampshire is facing, who will stand up to the recklessness of this administration, lower costs and make life better for Granite Staters,” he said in a debate last week.

Pappas frequently sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu despite Sununu once calling him a loser. He accused Sununu of having “a selective memory about what’s been going on over the last couple of years” and told him, “The guy who gave you his complete and total endorsement is wrecking New Hampshire’s Main Street economy.”

“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Pappas said. “This is not a moment to restore someone who was out of step with New Hampshire before and bring them back into power.”

Mike Bradley, 77, a licensed mental health counselor from Bow, described his vote for Pappas as “almost more anti- than pro-.”

“I’m so disgusted with what Republicans in general are doing with Trump at the helm, and pretty much no one’s standing up to him. The corruption, the homophobia, the transphobia, the endless war,” he said. “ I’m hoping that Democrats can grab a majority and counteract all this negative stuff.”

Sununu easily defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown and a handful of lesser-known candidates to win the Republican nomination. His first name was conspicuously absent from his green, blue and white campaign signs, and critics said he was counting on voters confusing him with his popular younger brother, Chris Sununu, who served eight years as governor. Their father also is a former governor.

Once the Senate’s youngest member, Sununu is now 62, older than Shaheen was when he bragged in a campaign advertisement about being younger and faster than she was. He derided Pappas as an ineffective and out-of-touch “career politician” despite the fact that Sununu traveled a similar path from the House to the Senate and comes from a family whose name is synonymous with Republican politics in New Hampshire.

“Chris Pappas talks about all the things he wants to do and wants to accomplish, but he’s been there for eight years and he hasn’t gotten the job done,” Sununu said during the debate. “I’ll focus on the right issues. I’ll stand up to my party and the president when it’s right for New Hampshire, and I’ll get things done.”

Campaign cash poured in from all sides, though data compiled by AdImpact and OpenSecrets.org showed Republicans were spending considerably more as the race tightened.

Republicans accused Pappas of catering to Washington lobbyists and party bosses, describing the race as “problem solver Sununu” vs. “puppet Pappas.” “New Hampshire needs a leader, not a lightweight,” one ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee concluded.

Pro-Pappas ads, meanwhile, accused Sununu of making millions off his political connections and highlighted the Sununu name appearing in the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Jeffrey Epstein said Sununu “has good stories.” It’s unclear whether he meant the current candidate or his father, John H. Sununu, but Sununu says neither of them ever met or communicated with Epstein or the recipient of the email.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Bookstore Owned by Sen. Wyden’s Wife to Pay $1.5M Over Pandemic Loan
entries.summary: The Strand Bookstore says the mistake was “unintentional” and that its accountant and lender were unaware of the restriction.
entries.content:
The Justice Department announced that a New York City bookstore owned by the wife of Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon will pay nearly $1.5 million to settle allegations it improperly obtained pandemic aid.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, accused Nancy Bass Wyden of lying on a February 2021 application to get a $932,350 second-round pandemic loan for her bookstore, despite rules passed by Congress barring such loans to businesses controlled by lawmakers or their spouses.

Ron Wyden, the Senate Finance Committee’s top Democrat, voted in favor of the legislation two months earlier.

Pirro said in a statement that the program was meant to save jobs, “not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator.”

“No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer,” she added.

The Strand Bookstore told CNBC the mistake was “unintentional” and that its accountant and lender were unaware of the restriction.

The $1.5 million civil settlement resolves a whistleblower lawsuit under the False Claims Act. Blockquote Inc., which brought the case, will receive approximately $148,256 from the settlement.
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Jon Ossoff, a Possible 2028 Presidential Candidate, Is Reelected to the Senate
entries.summary: The Georgia senator easily defeated Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff is projected to easily win reelection in the battleground state of Georgia, defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

Ossoff will enter his second term widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, given his track record as a prodigious fundraiser who has now twice pulled off statewide wins in a state where President Donald Trump has also won twice.

He has, however, repeatedly denied any interest in seeking the White House and promised to serve a full Senate term if reelected.

Ossoff far outspent his opponent and led in the polls throughout the campaign.

The senator has been a messaging leader for Democrats this cycle — he was early to adopt a populist focus on corruption, coined the term “Epstein class” and helped make Trump aide Natalie Harp a recognizable figure.

“Ossoff, especially when we are in a moment where a lot of the Democratic base and a lot of the Democratic electorate are hungry for a new generation of leadership … that just on paper creates an extremely compelling figure,” said Andrew Heaton, a Georgia Democratic operative. “Then throw in just how great of a speaker he is, how sharp he is.”

Collins, who won a competitive Republican primary with Trump’s endorsement by touting his MAGA bona fides, gambled on a base-turnout strategy by defending the Trump administration.

The lawmaker has a long history of posting inflammatory content on his X account and during the campaign faced a string of scandals involving his staff and family members’ ties to far-right views.

Ossoff framed his opponent as a “bigot” and in a debate said Collins had “hired half the Third Reich” to staff his office.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in the debate, invoking the late Georgia lawmaker and civil rights leader.

Collins’ failure to break through led national Republicans to abandon him — they deployed ad money to states seen as more winnable instead.

Georgia Republican operative Heath Garrett said that Collins’ brand as a MAGA warrior from rural Georgia was a mismatch for independents and swing voters.

“He's struggled to identify with and brand himself, in the suburban and urban areas along the coast and in the metro Atlanta area, because his personality and style don't necessarily fit those voters,” Garrett said.

Meanwhile, Ossoff’s efforts to cultivate relationships across party lines helped the incumbent woo Republicans.

“He has been methodical about working with elected officials in the smallest cities and counties throughout the state and trying to find ways to be helpful to them,” Garrett said. “And at the end of the day, constituent services still matter in politics, particularly in close elections.”
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: Troy Jackson Defeats Susan Collins for Maine Senate
entries.summary: That even Collins couldn’t pull off a win on Tuesday shows how widespread the backlash against Republicans was this midterm cycle.
entries.content:
Democrat Troy Jackson is projected to win Maine’s Senate race, ending Sen. Susan Collins’ five-term reign.

Collins styled herself as a moderate Republican who could disagree with President Donald Trump. That even she couldn’t pull off a win on Tuesday shows just how widespread the backlash against Republicans was this midterm cycle.

"It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a statement, adding that she had called Jackson to congratulate him.

When Collins started her first term in 1997, Republicans made up half of New England’s Senate delegation. By her last term, she was the only one left. Her defeat likely puts Maine’s seat out of reach for Republicans for the foreseeable future.

She defeated her Democratic opponent in 2020 — despite being massively outspent — and outperformed Trump, who lost in the state. This year, Collins was the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.

Collins ran her campaign as separately as possible from the national Republican Party, frequently highlighting her disagreements with the administration on tariffs, health care, and abortion access. Trump did not visit Maine to rally during the election, nor did Collins ask him to.

Collins pitched herself to Maine voters as a powerful advocate for the state, highlighting the funds she helped steer to the state through her role as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

She argued that while she could not stop the Trump agenda, she could help to insulate Maine from the worst impacts of it. In late October, she announced that she had convinced White House officials to exempt certain Canadian agricultural products from Trump’s tariffs. Heating oil costs, though, continued to climb as the Iran war continued toward Election Day.

Jackson, a former state Senate president, became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner dropped out of the race in July. Platner was accused of sexual assault, which he has denied.

While Jackson lacked some of Platner’s stage presence and outsider appeal, he presented himself as a reliable Democratic vote to stop Trump’s agenda.

Jackson relentlessly hammered Collins as an enabler of Trump’s economic and immigration policies. In a series of debates, he repeated that she voted with his agenda 95% of the time, blamed the senator for allowing tariffs against Canada to stand and said she “paid for the bullets” that an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer used in the killing of a Colombian man in Biddeford.

Jackson also criticized Collins over a ProPublica report released in September that revealed the FBI had previously investigated claims against Collins for a pay-to-play bribery scheme. The government did not bring charges against her, and she called the claims “completely false.”

Collins is one of two Senate Republicans who support abortion rights, and she had attacked Jackson for his previous support for anti-abortion bills. Jackson, however, argued that his stance had evolved and pointed out that Collins voted to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh even though he went on to vote to overturn Roe v. Wade. Collins said the court should not have overturned the decision, but declined to say that she regretted his confirmation.
entries.author: Chase Pellegrini de Paur

entries.title: Democrats Take Control of the Senate in a Rebuke of President Trump
entries.summary: Senate candidates across the country campaigned on the cost of living and corruption in government.
entries.content:
Democrats are projected to take control of the Senate after flipping seats in a striking number of solidly red states across the country, setting the party up to hold majorities in both chambers of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency.

Democrats won Senate seats in GOP strongholds like South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Iowa and Ohio and picked up a seat in North Carolina in a sharp rebuke of Trump’s policies. Midterm elections are often a referendum of the president’s leadership, but Democrats were able to secure remarkable wins in states that the president won by double digits in 2024.

The result was virtually unthinkable just a year ago, given how challenging this year’s map was for Democrats. But in South Carolina, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998, Democratic nominee and physician Annie Andrews is projected to win over Sen. Darline Graham — who took over the seat after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, passed away — in a stunning upset.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters and staff after the bulk of the Senate results came in that Democrats won because they listened to American families' concerns about “chaos and corruption” out on the campaign trail and recruited great candidates to run in red states.

“The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks,” Schumer said. “And as a result, there is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America now and on into the future. Americans voted for change and now Democrats must deliver.”

Texas state Rep. James Talarico’s double-digit victory over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton was another shining spot for Democrats, who have tried repeatedly to flip a Senate seat in the state that had not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber since 1988.

Democrats also picked up a seat in Kansas, where pastor Adam Hamilton unseated Sen. Roger Marshall in a state that a Democratic senator has not won since 1932.

Democrats also picked up a seat in Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown is projected to unseat Sen. Jon Husted. Brown lost his seat in 2024 after serving in Congress for more than three decades.

The forecast grew increasingly bleak for Republicans, who were looking to defend their majorities in both the House and Senate, as the night wore on. Trump’s low approval ratings, along with the high cost of food and fuel, exacerbated the tough political environment for the GOP.

Trump told The New York Times on Tuesday night that he was prepared to work with Democrats and accept the results of the midterm elections.

“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he said. “We’ll work with Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them.”

Overall spending in Senate races was over $3 billion, according to the most recent round of Federal Election Commission disclosures. Republicans outspent Democrats in their total investment in Senate races across the country, particularly in the most expensive races, pouring $300 million into Texas and more than $200 million into Ohio.

Democrats focused on affordability issues on the campaign trail, spotlighting how much more Americans are paying for everyday necessities since Republicans took control of the White House and Congress. In advertisements across the country, Democratic candidates warned that Republican-backed spending cuts enacted in 2025 have increased insurance premiums. They also highlighted corruption and ethics issues, vowing to pass a ban on congressional stock trading.

The Iran war also emerged as a prominent issue in the midterms, as repeated closures of the Strait of Hormuz led to rising gas, grocery and electricity prices.

Republicans, in turn, labeled Democrats as “socialists” and argued their ideas are out of step with American voters. They emphasized their signature tax-cut bill passed in July of 2025, which included provisions like no tax on tips, and the steep drop in border crossings under the Trump administration.

Democrats will now have to decide what their legislative agenda will look like in a unified Congress but a divided government, with the president unlikely to back most of their policy proposals. Jim Kessler, a Democratic strategist and executive vice president for policy at Third Way, said there’s a laundry list of priorities the party will be looking to tackle come January.

Kessler warned that Democrats in the next Congress should be careful to prioritize the issues that voters elected them to address, including the high cost of living, rather than trying to “create their own moments and their own headlines” with investigations of Trump officials.

Schumer is expected to retain his position leading the caucus, while Deputy Whip Brian Schatz is widely anticipated to become second in command, taking over for retiring Sen. Dick Durbin.

Schatz told The Washington Sun in an interview that Democrats would prioritize introducing legislation to end the war in Iran as well as restoring funding to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that was cut in 2025.

“We’re going to be a check against the excesses of this administration and the excesses of unified Republican control,” Schatz said. “There are going to be opportunities on a bipartisan basis to either delay or repeal portions of those cuts.”

“The things that voters care about are costs, so I would do something on tariffs and something on health care,” Kessler said. “But Democrats did a great job of tying corruption to people’s costs, and when you do investigations, you want to try to keep that connection there.”

Drew Littman, a Democratic strategist and a former Senate chief of staff, said that the work the Senate pursues in the next two years would likely lay the groundwork for the party’s case in the 2028 presidential race.

Littman said he’d advise lawmakers to avoid infighting over ideology and instead focus on writing legislation to revive expired Affordable Care Act subsidies, an issue Democrats shut down the government over in 2025.

“Focus on an agenda that directly answers many of the concerns that voters voice to us,” Littman said. “Do things that are very simple and understandable, that can at least get 50-plus-one votes in the Senate and majorities in the House that voters can point to and say, ‘Gee, if we had a Democratic president, I know at least those things would be done.’”

Some Democrats cast doubt on the idea that a Democratic-led Senate would be able to tackle affordability measures. Most legislation requires 60 votes to pass in the upper chamber, meaning that even with a majority, Democrats are unlikely to advance major policy legislation.

Littman predicted that much of the action in the Senate would revolve around Trump’s Cabinet, noting that those officials often leave during the second half of a lame-duck presidency.

“If Trump wants their replacements confirmed by the Senate, they're going to have to show up to hearings and testify, and Democrats can turn those hearings into oversight hearings,” Littman said. “I would anticipate maybe not in the first three months, but certainly in the first year, a lot of new nominees, a lot of new appointees, and some of them won't get confirmed.”

Littman added that much of the Republican-controlled Senate has been dedicated to confirming Trump’s slate of nominees, which is likely to change when Democrats hold a majority.

“The president won’t get a judge controlled in the next two years,” Littman said. “Resisting some of those appointees will be on the Democratic agenda, but that's driven by who resigns, who steps down, who passes away, and then what the president does about it.”
entries.author: Avani Kalra

entries.title: Trump Begged Voters to Pretend He Was on the Ballot. They Pummeled Him.
entries.summary: A stunning rebuke of Trump’s Republican Party left many on the right shaken and some questioning the president’s strategy.
entries.content:
Election night did not go President Donald Trump’s way. As the results trickled in from across the country, critical race after critical race went Democrats’ way. And pretty soon into the night, it was clear that Republicans would not only lose the House but also their grip on the Senate, too.

The White House was quick to cast blame on those not named Trump.

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official told The Washington Sun. “Also, candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves.”

But the loss, the full magnitude of which wasn’t fully clear Tuesday with many Western states still counting ballots, was nonetheless notable. It came after the president spent the final month of the election barnstorming the country, casting his 30 rallies in 20 states as the secret sauce to juice his base's turnout.

“Please pretend I’m on the freakin’ ballot,” Trump said in New York on Oct. 9. He said the same to crowds at most other October rallies.

In several red states, Trump talked about how hard he was working to elect Republican candidates. After Rep. Mike Collins’ Senate defeat in Georgia, a source close to the president said that Trump “busted his ass” for Collins, as he did for other candidates, and called Collins lazy for not working harder himself.

But Republicans have questioned for months whether Trump’s travel was doing any good, if not outright harming the candidates he was trying to help. One operative previously told The Sun that Trump just needed to “stay at the White House.”

When the poor showings spread across traditionally ruby red areas of the South — from Georgia to Texas and South Carolina — Republican operatives and officials again expressed annoyance with or questioned the White House’s strategy to parade an unpopular president into seemingly red races.

“The rallies didn’t matter,” said one Republican operative in Georgia. “It was all baked. People are fucking pissed and they blame him and they have good reason.”

One administration official said it plainly: “Bad message and bad candidates.”

A Trump world operative defended the logic behind the strategy, as Trump has widely been viewed as the magic charm for Republican turnout. But the plan underestimated the dissatisfaction with his presidency, even among people who supported him in the past.

“On one hand, the only person who owns the ‘Trump coalition’ and could, theoretically GOTV [get out the vote], is Trump,” one Republican operative said. “But also, the only person who owns an approval rating that is about to sink into the 20s is Trump.”

As the results came in, there was shock and denial, surprise and expletives flowing from all corners of the Republican Party. One administration official said they had just changed the channel on the TV they were watching to avoid more bad news.

Trump said that he would accept the election results.

“We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” Trump told The New York Times. “We’ll probably work something out.”

While Democrats appeared well on their way to asserting control over the next Congress, some in Trump’s orbit blamed the electoral disaster on the Iran war.

“Iran [was] a bigger problem than a lot of people realize,” a former Trump official said, pointing to persistently high gas prices. “I’d like to see the outcome with no Iran war. I do believe the Democrats would make [gains], but I don’t know that those gains would be like where they are in the Senate.”

Fox News host Sean Hannity, the staunchest of Trump allies, echoed that sentiment when asked whether the results would have been different without war.

“I don’t think there’s any doubt about it,” Hannity said. “Unfortunately, it’s the best thing for our children and grandchildren. But higher gas prices, how people feel, I think, is the more dominant feeling force right now.”

Rather than being an indictment of Trump, a source in Trump world told The Sun that the night’s results were proof that Republicans can’t take turnout for granted when Trump isn’t on the ballot.

“President Trump and his operation worked harder than anyone to turn out Republican voters, going above and beyond to make up for some candidates who failed to do the work themselves,” the source said, predicting that independents who swung Democrat would have buyer’s remorse.

Those in Trump’s orbit didn’t expect the president to spend much time reflecting on his role in the blowout.

Some advisers saw the reactions coming ahead of Tuesday night.

“If we lose the election, someone whose last name is not Trump is gonna take the blame,” one outside adviser to Trump told The Sun.

It was a sentiment that Trump began to lay out online shortly after the first polls closed, attacking Fox News’ reporting on the races in multiple social media posts.

“It’s them, not me,” Trump said of Fox on Truth Social. “My numbers are better than they have ever been.”

And even after many lost races, he remained resolute in his stance.

“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” Trump said later. “Thank you for your attention to this matter.”
entries.author: Jasmine Wright, Ben T.N. Mause, Ayah Ali-Ahmad

entries.title: Josh Turek Wins Iowa Senate Seat in a Major Flip for Democrats
entries.summary: The Democrat’s win adds to a quickly-growing list of improbable victories in Senate races.
entries.content:
State Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat, is projected to win Iowa’s Senate seat, giving his party more hope in the Midwest.

The state, for years seen as a Republican party stronghold, emerged as a surprise battleground this cycle.

In the final weeks leading up to Election Day, polling between Turek and Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, his opponent for the open Senate seat, was tight. Democrats looking to expand the Senate map saw Iowa as unusually vulnerable for Republicans and poured money into the state in support of Turek. Former President Barack Obama, whose path to the presidency was propelled by Iowa, even appeared in an ad endorsing Turek.

During the primary, Turek made the case that he could appeal to voters across the political spectrum. He pointed to flipping a state house seat in a district that voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump in 2016, 2020 and 2024 as evidence of his electability.

That strategy continued into the general election, where he made a point of emphasizing his track record of working with Republicans in the state Legislature. He also made overtures to the state’s rural communities, including by focusing on the strain high gas prices have put on the farming industry.

“When I joined the Iowa Legislature … I built strange bedfellows. I built relationships across the aisle,” Turek said during an Oct. 7 debate. “I believe more than even Republican versus Democrat, what Iowans want is they want someone that is going to go up and work hard to provide solutions to people's problems through bipartisan policy.”

State Rep. Elinor Levin, a Democrat who endorsed Turek and served alongside him in the state house, told The Washington Sun that she believes Turek will avoid “getting hung up on culture wars or on us-versus-them politics” while in Congress.

“I think Iowa needs someone who's going to be a voice at the table,” Levin said. “[He] understands from a personal perspective what it is like to struggle and to have to work hard to build a life for yourself.”

Hinson, who was seen as one of Republicans’ most promising recruits this cycle, attempted to distance herself from the president on some issues in the race’s final months. Hinson was critical when asked about Trump’s deal with Russia for oil, and she also broke with the president in speaking against the war in Iran. In June, Politico obtained audio of Hinson warning that the war would become a “political liability” if it did not end before the midterms.

“I don't want this to be a forever war,” Hinson said during one of her debates against Turek. “I trust in our U.S. military, the greatest fighting force in the world, to bring this to a close as quickly as possible.”

In October, she appeared alongside the president in the Oval Office during the announcement of a massive steel plant planned for Southeast Iowa, though the deal is no sure thing.

Iowa’s elections this year were also marked by a deep focus on the state’s cancer crisis, with candidates across parties for offices up and down the ballot pitching plans to reverse Iowa’s cancer rates.

“I think more and more people are paying attention to who actually cares about the health care crisis and the cancer crisis and the water quality crisis, and who is legitimately going to address it,” Turek told The Sun in late October.

During the general election, Turek characterized Hinson as a political insider, including by accusing her husband of operating as a “shadow lobbyist.” The Sun previously reported on documents that showed Hinson’s husband was credited with arranging meetings between insurance industry lobbyists and lawmakers including Hinson.

Turek will fill the Senate seat left vacant by Sen. Joni Ernst, who served two terms in the Senate.

In 2025, Democrats flipped a state Senate seat in a Republican-leaning district in a special election, breaking Republicans’ supermajority. Turek’s victory indicates that the Republican grip on the state may have weakened even further since, leaving an opening for Democrats willing to appeal to voters on both sides of the aisle.

“We saw that once again, Iowa truly is not a red state, not a blue state,” Levin said. “Things break on very close margins pretty frequently here.”
entries.author: Emma Ruby

entries.title: Kansas Just Elected a Democratic Senator for the First Time in Nearly 100 Years
entries.summary: Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, has unseated Republican Roger Marshall in another major upset.
entries.content:
For the first time in nearly a century, Kansas is sending a Democrat to Washington.

Adam Hamilton, the Methodist pastor of a Kansas City-area megachurch, is projected to beat Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an upset that will make him the first Democrat from Kansas elected to the U.S. Senate since 1932 — the year Franklin D. Roosevelt won his first term as president.

Speaking to supporters Tuesday night, Hamilton peppered his speech with lines from scripture, calling for compassion, kindness, decency and bipartisanship.

“We are not flyover country,” Hamilton said. “We are the heart of America, and we have a message to send. And part of that message, truly, is we are better together than we are divided.”

Marshall ran on his previous experience as an OB-GYN. But that career came to haunt him as his lawsuits against patients to recover medical debts, which in some cases led to them being arrested, became a major campaign issue. Marshall also lacked a robust ground game and reported poor fundraising numbers. A last-minute intervention by national Republicans wasn’t enough to rescue him.

David Kensinger, a lobbyist and veteran Kansas GOP operative, called Marshall’s campaign a “failure to launch,” pointing to factors like his third-quarter fundraising haul, a measly $800,000.

“I think everyone expected that an incumbent senator under threat, in the third quarter of his election year … was going to raise a significant amount of cash,” Kensinger said. “And $800,000 is an astonishing shortfall.”

Marshall also faced criticism over how much time he spent at his second home in Florida.

By the time of the final Senate debate on Oct. 21, Marshall acknowledged that it was a competitive race and pleaded for “Trump voters to come out.”

“Control of the Senate comes through Kansas,” he said onstage.

Bob Beatty, a political scientist at Washburn University in Topeka, said the medical debt storyline and associated attack ads undermined the image of a senator who styled himself as “Doc Marshall.”

“Your local, friendly country doctor is charging you 18% interest on your new baby. And it’s had legs,” Beatty said of the storyline, adding that the line of attack the Hamilton campaign picked up was “effective.”

Marshall cut a video late in the campaign trying to respond to the medical debt issue, reportedly against the wishes of his advisers.
Election 2026 Kansas Senate (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)The senator’s campaign also faced questions about whether he violated ethics rules by using official Senate staff as an extension of his campaign. His most recent fundraising reports lacked any indication that he employed full-time campaign staff. It also added to a perception that he wasn’t taking his reelection campaign seriously.

Congressional staffers can work on campaigns, but only if they follow strict guidelines.

“But you also need people who are setting up literature drops and organizing get-out-the-vote efforts and raising money, and that takes real people who do real work,” Kensinger said. “And if you don't have them, there's a danger the work doesn't get done.”

President Donald Trump, who visited the state the weekend before Election Day, also created headaches for Marshall, who sought to rally the president’s base while acknowledging how the administration’s policies were felt on the ground.

The Iran war drove up diesel prices for farmers, while immigration raids and Trump’s move to open up beef markets hurt ranchers. Amid the trade war with Canada, Trump threatened Bombardier, a Montreal-based aerospace company with a major presence in Wichita.

Marshall did not separate himself far from Trump, telling voters last month that “this is one of the best economies I've ever seen in my lifetime."

Hamilton outraised Marshall, entering October with a 3-to-1 cash advantage.

The soft-spoken pastor distanced himself from national Democrats, saying he wouldn’t support Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader and that he didn’t want former Vice President Kamala Harris to campaign for him in Kansas.

 

Hamilton, a onetime Republican who considered running for Senate as an independent, promised to serve Kansas the same way he serves the nation’s largest Methodist congregation — by “leading from the middle.”

Beatty said Hamilton smartly hammered his moderate message and communicated it well.

“Not all pastors are great communicators, but many are, and [Hamilton] certainly is,” Beatty said. “He knows how to talk to people and talk to the camera and address groups right out the bat.”

—
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: Caps Lose to the Stars, 6-5, as Comeback Bid Falls Short
entries.summary: Jordan Kyrou scored a goal and had two assists for Washington, which fought back from a 4-0 deficit.
entries.content:
Jason Robertson scored the third-fastest natural hat trick in team history to help the Dallas Stars to a 6-5 victory over the Washington Capitals on Tuesday night.

Robertson’s sixth, seventh and eighth goals of the season came in a stretch of 5 minutes, 20 seconds early in the second period. His last, a snap shot from the point through traffic to make it 4-0, chased Capitals goaltender Logan Thompson with 14:17 to go until the second intermission.

Mikko Rantanen scored later in the second period to tie Robertson for the team lead as Dallas picked up points for a fifth consecutive road game.

Roope Hintz scored and added an assist, and Joel Kirvanta struck first for Dallas midway through the first period. Jake Oettinger had 20 saves.

Jordan Kyrou scored a goal and had two assists for Washington, which eventually closed the deficit to 6-5 on Ryan Leonard’s goal on a six-on-five with 1:02 remaining.

Boone Jenner, Jakob Chychrun and Justin Sourdif also scored in the Capitals’ second straight home loss. Dylan Strome contributed his team-leading 10th and 11th assists.

Robertson’s hat trick started only 23 seconds into the second when he skated uncontested into the left faceoff circle and beat Thompson to his near glove side on the power play.

For his second, he took Arrtu Hyry’s drop-off pass, cut back to avoid Chychrun’s body check along the right boards, then fired the puck between Thompson and his far post.

Washington responded by scoring the fourth and fifth goals this season against Dallas’ penalty kill and closing to within 5-3 by the end of the second period. Sourdif made it 6-4 with 7:05 left in the third.

Up Next

Capitals: Complete a three-game homestand Saturday against Florida.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Democrat Rob Sand Wins Election to be Iowa’s Next Governor
entries.summary: Sand defeated Zach Lahn, a first-time candidate who surprised even members of his own party when he won the Republican primary.
entries.content:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa voters chose Democrat Rob Sand to be their next governor, flipping the seat Republicans have held for more than two decades and likely ushering in a new era of divided state government.

Sand defeated Zach Lahn, a first-time candidate who surprised even members of his own party when he won the Republican primary. Sand, who is currently state auditor, has been the only Democrat serving in statewide elected office.

His victory will almost certainly make him a leading face of a Democratic Party that he’s kept at arm’s length, focusing instead on his middle-of-the-road approach to politics and his small-town upbringing. But Democrats have been eager to claw back territory in Midwestern and rural states where they’ve struggled in recent years.

The two candidates campaigned on criticisms of the state’s status quo following a decade of Republican control under retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds. Both highlighted the state’s stagnant economy, declines in public education and uniquely high and rising rates of cancer diagnoses.

But they offered voters starkly different visions for the office and solving those problems.

The open race — in a midterm when Republicans faced national headwinds — shook up Iowa’s recent political conventional wisdom and revived the state as battleground territory, despite Republicans outnumbering Democrats among party-affiliated registered voters.

Reynolds’ unexpected retirement opened up the first governor’s race in the state without an incumbent since 2010. While Sand was ultimately unopposed on the Democratic primary ballot, Republicans had to first get through a five-way primary.

Sand, 44, often laments the way the country’s political system forces people to pick sides, even as he has only run for office as a Democrat and has donated substantially to the party. He acknowledged he’d likely have to work with Republican majorities in the state House and Senate, saying divided government would be good for solving problems.

He criticized Republicans for ignoring a worsening budget deficit that’s emerged from their tax cuts and investment in education savings accounts, which provide students with public dollars to pay for private school tuition.

But he acknowledged he’d likely have to work with Republican majorities in the state House and Senate, saying divided government would be good for solving problems. He said he’d also be a check on Republican efforts to push culture war bills.

In a sign of the race’s competitiveness, many of Iowa’s prominent industry groups in agriculture and business declined to weigh in on the contest, endorsing in other contests but not the governor’s race.

Lahn’s general election campaign was scaled up quickly after his surprise win in the June primary. He had five months to introduce himself to voters, including many Republicans, and to dramatically increase his fundraising and campaign staff.

Lahn won the primary by less than a percentage point over U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump. In the five-way race, he prevailed with only about a third of Republican voters supporting him.

Lahn was not shy about pushing back on traditional Iowa GOP positions. He boasted that he had already been successful in changing the narrative within the Republican Party and emphasized that Iowa couldn’t be succeeding — even under GOP leadership — if it’s losing its family farms, its young people to other states, its residents to cancer and its achievements in public education.

Still, toe-to-toe with Sand in debates, Lahn leaned on traditional party positions, saying Sand would be a liberal governor who would raise taxes, increase regulations and push a political agenda in public education.

As was the case in his previous two elections to be auditor, Sand prevailed in a statewide race just two years after Iowa voters backed Trump.

Much of the party’s hopes for restoring Democratic leadership to the state rested on Sand despite his efforts to keep his distance from party politics. Sand won his last election by a razor-thin margin — fewer than 3,000 votes — but he has outperformed other Democrats in both of his races, especially in rural areas.

Sand worked for years to build a likable public profile by holding annual county town halls, publicizing his findings both as a former state prosecutor and as auditor, and being active on social media. That included posting about what he was eating around the state, nodding at his small-town northeast Iowa upbringing and sharing his bowhunting escapades.

Sand contrasted his personal life with Lahn’s, hitting Lahn for his ties outside of the state and for only registering to vote in Iowa two years ago, just before the deadline to run as a candidate in this election. Lahn has explained frequent flights to Kansas as a result of his blended family, which he says won’t affect his ability to govern. Lahn and his wife, Annie, both have children from previous marriages who do not currently live full-time in Iowa.

By contrast, Lahn criticized Sand for the millions of dollars that his wife and in-laws have contributed to his campaign and called him a career politician. Sand was a prosecutor under a Democratic state attorney general before running for auditor in 2018. That ultimately did not drive away voters at the polls.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Sherrod Brown Flips Ohio Senate Seat in a Key Win for Democrats
entries.summary: Brown defeated incumbent Sen. Jon Husted to serve out the remainder of Vice President Vance’s term.
entries.content:
Sherrod Brown is returning to the Senate.

The Ohio Democrat is projected to defeat incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the seat once held by Vice President JD Vance. Brown, who previously served three terms in the Senate before losing reelection in 2024 to Bernie Moreno, will serve out the remaining two years of Vance’s term.

Brown’s victory is an important one for Democrats in the state, who have steadily lost power in every election since 2012. President Donald Trump won Ohio by 11 percentage points in 2024.

This year, however, Democrats found success with an electorate angry about high prices and a booming data center industry in the state. Brown, who benefitted from having strong name recognition, tapped into those frustrations on the campaign trail.

“The first thing we do is end the war, period,” Brown said during an Oct. 21 campaign rally. “Second thing we do is get rid of the tariffs. Third thing that we do is we begin to clean up the corruption in Columbus and in Washington.”

Brown referred to his opponent as “the face of data centers,” and accused Husted of giving tax breaks to the developments during his tenure as lieutenant governor. In the month leading up to the election, Brown’s campaign sponsored billboards near data centers that read “Jon Husted did that.”
20261028_mcgarvey_OHGOP_3773.jpg (8004x5339, AR: 1.50)Brown also took a different approach toward the president. In 2020 and 2021, Brown voted to convict Trump on impeachment charges. In the campaign's final stretch, he said he would not support a third impeachment attempt “no matter what happens in the midterms.”

“He gets a lot of crossover appeal from moderates, from centrists, from progressives that support him,” David Brock, the chair of the Cuyahoga County Democratic Party, told The Washington Sun.

Democrats threw high-profile surrogates onto the campaign trail to help pull Brown over the line. Less than two weeks before Election Day, Brown campaigned in Cleveland alongside former President Barack Obama.

Still, Republicans outspent Democrats by millions after Labor Day, and doubled down on investing into the state until the end. A cryptocurrency-adjacent PAC had dropped $55 million against Brown as of Oct. 21, and Husted was one of several Republican candidates boosted during the last-minute MAGA Inc. blitz that began in late October.

Trump and Vance made several trips to the state and campaigned alongside Husted, who they praised as a consummate conservative. Trump’s backing of Husted dominated the headlines after he repeatedly praised Husted’s “ass” at campaign stops across the country.

That commentary did not prove powerful enough to drive Republicans to the polls.

Ohio’s Republican secretary of state, Frank LaRose, told The Sun that he believed any Republican losses could be chalked up to low voter turnout.

“The 1980s rock band Rush had a song called ‘Free Will,’ and in that song there's a line: If you choose not to decide, you still have made a choice,” LaRose said. “Voter turnout matters. Elections have consequences.”
entries.author: Emma Ruby

entries.title: Democrat Shomari Figures Wins Reelection to U.S. House in Alabama's 2nd Congressional District
entries.summary: Figures defeated Republican Rhett Marques.
entries.content: Democratic incumbent Shomari Figures won election Tuesday to the U.S. House of Representatives representing Alabama's 2nd Congressional District, defeating Republican Rhett Marques. Figures, an attorney and former Obama administration staffer, secured a second term in the southern Alabama district despite a redrawing of its boundaries to favor Republicans. The redistricting was part of a nationwide effort by President Donald Trump to maximize his party's chances of holding onto its slim House majority this year. The new map was enabled by a U.S. Supreme Court decision in April that weakened part of the Voting Rights Act. Marques was the longtime owner of an auto service business. The Associated Press declared Figures the winner at 11:00 p.m. EST.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Democrats Take Texas
entries.summary: Democrat James Talarico won a seat to the U.S. Senate, making him the first Democrat to win a statewide seat in the state in 32 years.
entries.content:
AUSTIN — James Talarico is projected to become Texas’ first statewide elected Democrat in more than three decades, defeating state Attorney General Ken Paxton in the most watched and most expensive Senate race in history.

The victory is a landmark moment for the Democratic Party, which has spent years attempting to wrestle control of Texas away from Republicans and predicting that the state’s changing demographics would eventually allow it to do so.

While Democrats were optimistic going into Tuesday evening, when it became clear Talarico would win, the energy at the election night watch party with the candidate was palpable.

During a concession speech given late Tuesday, Paxton said he’d be “praying” for Talarico. Paxton said he was grateful for "the opportunity to try to do the best I could to do good for Texas" during his 12 years as the state’s attorney general.

“I love Texas, I’ll always love Texas. We will still fight for this place,” Paxton said. “We've had a difficult night tonight across the country, but it’s not over.”

Throughout the campaign, Talarico, a two-term state representative, merged messages of faith and populism. He made a case to independent and Republican voters who were turned off by the Trump administration and Paxton that he could be a candidate for all kinds of Texans.

Talarico leaned on hometown nostalgia. He appeared alongside country singers Kacey Musgraves and The Chicks, and branded himself with “Friday Night Lights”-inspired messaging. He touted endorsements by members of the Bush family and Thomas J. Henry, a well-known personal injury attorney who backed Paxton during the Republican primary.

“I am tired of us being divided into teams, left versus right, blue versus red, urban versus rural,” Talarico said during a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media in October. “Because the truth is, we're all on the same team.”

Talarico consistently polled ahead of Paxton throughout the race. In the election’s final weeks, Republican donors, including Elon Musk, began dumping hundreds of millions of dollars into the race to support Paxton.

The Sen. Chuck Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC waded into the race in September, when it began an advertising blitz against Paxton. Home to 20 different media markets, Texas is among the most expensive states to campaign in, and the super PAC had hoped to focus spending on smaller, cheaper states, The New York Times reported.

Talarico was able to pull off the upset in part because Paxton was weighed down with his own baggage.

Over the course of the campaign, Paxton faced criticism over unforced errors: Leaked audio in which he was critical of his own party repeatedly became a focal point, and in October, The Wall Street Journal published footage that showed Paxton partying in Dubai with U.S. fugitives.

His wife, who filed for divorce “on biblical grounds” last year, appeared in an ad encouraging voters to support Republican candidates, though she did not name Paxton. Incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton defeated in a runoff election, declined to offer his endorsement. Paxton’s 2023 impeachment (and acquittal) by his own party, haunted the campaign.

Still, Paxton tried to rile his base by painting Talarico as too liberal for the state.

“If we lose Texas, we lose America,” was a regular refrain at Paxton’s campaign rallies.

At 37 years old, Talarico will be the youngest member of the Senate. He appealed broadly to younger voters at a time when skepticism toward the gerontocracy, and entrenched Washington politicians, was on the rise.

Talarico pledged to tackle issues related to affordability, education access and the growing class divide once sworn in.

—
Editor's Note: This story was updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Emma Ruby, Daniella Diaz

entries.title: Democrat Paige Cognetti Defeats Incumbent in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District
entries.summary: Cognetti is the mayor of Scranton.
entries.content: Democrat Paige Cognetti won election Tuesday to the U.S. House of Representatives representing Pennsylvania's 8th Congressional District, defeating Republican incumbent Rob Bresnahan. Cognetti is the mayor of Scranton. She campaigned as an independent-minded Democrat and corruption-fighting city leader. Bresnahan was unable to convince voters that he deserved a second term in Washington. The Associated Press declared Cognetti the winner at 10:41 p.m. EST.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Democrats Win Control of the House in Shocking Sweep Across the Country
entries.summary: The midterm election was a striking referendum on President Donald Trump’s leadership two years into his second term.
entries.content:
Democrats are projected to win control of the House of Representatives in a stunning sweep, ending unified Republican control of Washington in a stark rebuke of President Donald Trump’s leadership.

The margin of the win is still unclear, with a number of contested seats still yet to be called. Midterm elections are often a referendum on the president’s leadership, but Democrats were able to secure a striking number of wins in deep-red districts that the president won by double digits in 2024.

Rep. Richard Hudson (R-North Carolina), the current head of the House Republicans’ campaign arm, is trailing in his race in what has been a solidly red district.

Democrat Zach Dembo flipped a highly watched seat in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, an area that Trump won by 15 percentage points in 2024. Democrat Jamie Ager won North Carolina’s 11th District, which Trump won by nearly 10 points, following a series of misconduct allegations against Rep. Chuck Edwards, who withdrew from the race earlier this year. And Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti won Rep. Rob Bresnahan’s contested Pennsylvania seat, a district that swung for Trump in 2024 by 8 points.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries took a victory lap in a speech to Democrats and reporters on Tuesday night in Washington.

“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries said. “From sea to shining sea, the American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption. They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January.”

Democratic campaigns focused intensely on the cost of living in the fight over the House this year, blaming Trump and Republicans for high prices due to tariffs and the Iran war. Costs generated by data centers and artificial intelligence were also a central part of the argument against the GOP, often mentioned alongside allegations of corruption benefiting the president and billionaires.

The result is a major setback for Trump halfway through his second term, handing power to Democrats to block his agenda and launch investigations into an administration that has so far faced little pushback from a Republican-controlled Congress.

House Speaker Mike Johnson conceded that his party had lost their majority while speaking to reporters in his hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana. He noted that the party in power typically does not keep seats during the midterms, adding that this year, “history will be kept.”

But Johnson touted his efforts to support GOP candidates in the midterm elections. “Since becoming speaker, I can’t believe I’m about to tell you. I’ve raised more than $870 million, which makes me, I think, the largest fundraiser in the history of the Republican Party, other than President Trump,” Johnson said. “Come 2028, we will take back the House.”

And, Democrats stunning wins in red states on Tuesday came even after the GOP kicked off a redistricting push to add Republican seats in states like Texas, Florida and North Carolina earlier this year. Democrats were largely able to buck those efforts on Tuesday night, holding on and ousting Republicans in several of those redrawn districts.

The Democratic victory also means Jeffries will likely become the first Black speaker of the House next year. He would be the first Democrat to hold the position since his mentor and the first woman to hold the office, Rep. Nancy Pelosi, relinquished the gavel in 2023.

Through nearly two years of complete control over Washington, Trump and Republicans were able to pass a sweeping bill that extended tax cuts from the first Trump administration, slashed billions in spending for Medicaid and food assistance and poured funding into immigration enforcement and border security. They also clawed back funding for foreign aid programs and public broadcasting.

It’s the second time Democrats have reclaimed the House during a midterm election under a Trump administration. In 2018, Democrats won 41 Republican seats, taking the majority and later impeaching Trump twice.

Democrats have promised to investigate the president, his family and his close circle of allies. That includes an expanded congressional investigation into the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his network of connections. Many are wary of impeaching Trump a third time, but other officials such as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be in their sights.

Leaders have said they want to focus on the issues that helped them win. They’ve already started to sketch out a House Democratic agenda for next year, campaigning on reversing some of the GOP’s deepest cuts to programs like Medicaid and SNAP, restoring Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies and seeking to end the war in Iran. They will have a hard time enacting that agenda, though, with any legislation passing the House also having to go through the Senate and receive Trump’s signature (or enough votes to override a veto).

The win for House Democrats comes with a slew of new headaches and challenges for the party’s leadership.

Jeffries’ caucus will get an influx of progressives who are pushing to move their party to the left and challenge its leadership. A number of Democrats who refused to publicly support Jeffries for speaker during their campaigns won their races. The growing progressive bloc could present challenges for Jeffries in the speakership. The New York Democrat and members of his inner circle have already started outreach to potential defectors.

Democrats claimed control of the House in spite of an aggressive, nationwide mid-decade redistricting campaign spearheaded by the president to bolster his party’s chances. GOP-led states, led by Texas, redrew congressional maps to give Republicans an advantage in more than a dozen districts. Democrats retaliated with redistricting of their own in California and other states, but Republicans emerged from the redistricting battle with an advantage.

The Democratic triumph also sinks the House Republican Conference into uncertainty. Johnson’s political future is up in the air, and there’s a roster of potentially interested suitors for the minority leader job.

Johnson’s tenure as speaker will end after three turbulent years, in which he struggled to balance demands from the president, a rowdy faction of House conservatives and the realities of governing.
entries.author: Stephen Neukam, Avani Kalra

entries.title: Democrat Zach Dembo Flips Seat in Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District
entries.summary: Dembo is a former federal prosecutor and U.S. Navy lawyer.
entries.content: Democrat Zach Dembo won election Tuesday to the U.S. House of Representatives representing Kentucky's 6th Congressional District, defeating Republican Ralph Alvarado. Dembo won in a strongly Republican district to replace Republican Rep. Andy Barr, who vacated the seat to run for the U.S. Senate. Dembo is a former federal prosecutor and U.S. Navy lawyer. He was backed by the Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Alvarado is a physician who was the first Hispanic person to serve in the state legislature. The Associated Press declared Dembo the winner at 10:16 p.m. EST.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Democrats Score a Stunning Senate Win in South Carolina
entries.summary: Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, blocked the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister from winning a full term.
entries.content:
This seat wasn’t on even the most optimistic of Democrats’ wish lists at the start of the cycle.

Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, is projected to unseat South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham, sister of the late Lindsey Graham, in a shocking upset. This gives Democrats a Senate seat in South Carolina for the first time in decades.

Andrews ran on lowering costs, tying Graham to President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and high prices for gas and groceries. She promised to stand up to Democrats when she disagreed and to work with Republicans to cut taxes.

Graham was appointed to the Senate after her brother’s unexpected death. Republicans knew little about her even as Trump and many party members quickly lined up behind her. Andrews painted her as the president’s “puppet.”

“Nobody in Washington recruited me to run,” Andrews told supporters Tuesday. “Nobody handed me a seat in the United States Senate. And nobody wrote me a script. I owe no one in Washington anything, I owe South Carolina everything.”

National Republicans tried to go to Graham’s rescue with more than $5 million from the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune. It was a surprising move to shore up a Senate seat in a state that supported Trump by 18 percentage points two years ago, as were the trips in the final weeks of the campaign that Trump took to the state to try to rally the base.

Those efforts fell short.

Katon Dawson, a strategist and former chair of the state GOP, said before Election Day that a more established candidate wouldn’t have struggled against Andrews.

“If it had been Mark Sanford or if it would have been Ralph Norman, I don't think there'd be a contest,” Dawson said. “Those were professional politicians ready to go, ready to debate, ready to do everything.”

“She's a sweet person,” Dawson said of Graham. “She's not a politician. She never wanted to get in the limelight.”

Still, Dawson predicted a narrow Graham victory ahead of Election Day.

"In ruby red South Carolina, people are pissed off at Donald Trump,” Dawson said Tuesday night, shortly before the race was called for Andrews. “And we didn't see that one coming."

New to politics, Graham had to go through a late-summer special primary and an Aug. 25 primary runoff, only narrowly defeating Rep. Ralph Norman to clinch the nomination. Her inexperience showed throughout the campaign, epitomized during a primary debate gaffe in which she admitted she was “not that informed on national security” when asked about Taiwan.

Andrews was also far more successful in the fundraising race. Her campaign raised $24.2 million through mid-October, while Graham’s campaign raised just $1.9 million.

Andrews distanced herself from national Democrats, at one point telling reporters that she didn’t want any of them to head there to campaign for her.

She also took out an ad saying she opposed gender-affirming surgery for minors and that transgender athletes should play on teams based on their sex assigned at birth — Trump and Graham both cast Andrews as a candidate supportive of transgender rights, and Trump incorporated a transphobic slur into his nickname for Andrews.

Speaking before Election Day, Trav Robertson, former chair of the state Democratic Party, said he saw a lack of enthusiasm for Graham and predicted the race would boil down to economic issues.

“[Voters] understand what's happening to this economy, and the overarching issue is we are in a war that we didn't need to be in,” Robertson said. “South Carolina, Alabama, Mississippi, Oklahoma, they are not immune to the high prices of diesel. They're not immune to the high price of gas.”

—
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Hunter Riggall

entries.title: After a Dramatic Final Stretch, Robert White Wins D.C. Delegate Race
entries.summary: White, who resigned from the D.C. Council on Monday, was elected to replace longtime Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton.
entries.content:
Former At-Large D.C. Council member Robert White became the third nonvoting congressional delegate in D.C.’s history on Tuesday. The Democratic lawmaker will replace Eleanor Holmes Norton, who represented the District for 18 terms.

“These are hard, nearly impossible shoes to fill,” White told The Washington Sun. “But I think [voters] feel like if someone can do it, maybe I can.”

White claimed an overwhelming lead shortly after polls closed on Tuesday. The D.C. Board of Elections reported that he had won 87% of votes counted by 9:30 p.m. The victory marks the end of a hectic final campaign stretch for White, who resigned from the council Monday. The last-minute dramatics stemmed from a 1970 law that mandates that any person elected as D.C. congressional delegate must not occupy a paid political position on the day of their election.

Supporters filled The Delegate in Northwest D.C. on Tuesday night, setting a celebratory tone from the very start of the night. With DJ EZ Street spinning hip-hop and classic go-go, White danced his way into the watch party. 

But the room hushed as 89-year-old Norton made her entrance. Well-wishers lined up to take photos with the longtime lawmaker, and White spoke about her importance to the District. 

“As a kid growing up in this city, you showed us what it meant to fight for our city, to serve our city,” he told her. “Thank you for the opportunity to be your legislative counsel, to learn from you and to stand here because of you.” 

In his acceptance speech, he spoke about supporting locals who remain impacted by federal cutbacks and continuing his push for D.C. statehood. 

“My ambition is to be [D.C.’s] last delegate because we will turn this seat into one with a vote, and we will create two more in the Senate,” he said. “We will get full power and equal standing in our democracy because we deserve it.”

Earlier on Tuesday, a small group of residents began congregating outside of Shepherd Elementary School in Northwest D.C., hoping to greet their much-discussed neighbor as he cast his own ballot.

White was accompanied by his wife and their two young daughters. He wore black slacks, a crisp white button-down, gray New Balances and a cap embroidered with three names: Fauntroy, Norton and White. Walter Fauntroy was the delegate before Norton.

“Growing up in D.C. and feeling looked over as a family, but also as a city — now I get to go to Congress and represent us,” he said after voting. “Nationally, people are tired of losing close votes that they could win if we had two senators and a voting member of the House from the District of Columbia, so I think this is a time where statehood is a mandate nationally.”
2026-11-3 Midterm Election Coverage (Washington Sun)-59.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)2026-11-3 Midterm Election Coverage (Washington Sun)-50.jpg (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)White has spent time advocating for D.C. statehood during rallies for fellow Democrats in nearby states. He says he believes the country is finally ready to embrace the District as a state.

“They don't want to see people of the District of Columbia continue to be disenfranchised just because of who we might vote for,” he said.

Shepherd Park resident Kim D’Abreu cast her ballot for White (and Janeese Lewis George in the mayoral race) with a similar thought in mind.

“We're looking for leadership, especially since the District is disenfranchised in so many ways,” she said. “We need a powerful presence in Washington, and they both seem like the candidates to do meaningful work in that way.”

Another big fan of White’s stood just outside the polling area. Robert White Sr., the electee’s father, said he was proud to hear his son telling a reporter that politics can be a “social justice ministry” if done correctly.

The elder White remembers the young boy who shied away from the public eye after being severely wounded in a near-fatal car accident. But he said he believes that period is when White established a passion for making his city “whole” again.

“I think that's where he began to develop his voice,” he said. “That people would hear him — even if they could see the scars, they could hear his passion, hear his voice. Now that voice is for the people of Washington, D.C.”

White Sr., who said he has been on the corner near the elementary school every Election Day over the past 12 years, advocating for his son, will soon watch that boy take his place in Congress.

“My dad didn't leave me a big inheritance, but what he left me was his name,” White Sr. said of his own father. “And his name is still good around this city.”
entries.author: Shamira Muhammad

entries.title: D.C. Votes to Ban Foie Gras in a Win for Animal Rights Activists
entries.summary: Voters swung in favor of Initiative 86 on Tuesday, meaning that the production and sale of foie gras will soon be banned in the District.
entries.content:
Foie gras is foie-gone.

D.C. voters swung in favor of Initiative 86 on Tuesday, meaning that the production and sale of foie gras, a French delicacy that is produced by force-feeding ducks and geese, will soon be banned in the District.

The result is a victory for the group of animal rights activists that had pushed for its passage and comes as some prominent chefs and restaurateurs made a last-minute push against the initiative.

The effort began just a year ago, when the D.C. Board of Elections gave the go-ahead to the ballot initiative supported by Pro-Animal Future, a nonprofit organization that has advocated for a variety of ballot measures across the country.

At the local level, aligned animal rights nonprofits have used protests — and live animals like Olivia Gray, a pet duck — to advocate to pass the initiative. Activists have pointed to studies indicating that the farm practice of producing foie gras — which involves force-feeding fowl — harms animals.

When the election results were announced at the watch party for D.C. Council candidate Oye Owolewa at Solly's bar in Shaw — where supporters of Pro-Animal D.C. had been invited to share the space — the crowd had much to celebrate. In addition to Initiative 86 passing, Owolewa won an at-large seat for D.C. Council.

Owelewa, one of the campaign’s earliest elected supporters, said he was looking forward to helping the council shape enforcement around the issue.

“I'm excited to be on the forefront and ... figuring out what it means for us in 2027,” Owolewa told The Washington Sun.

Not long after Owolewa delivered a victory speech, Olivia the duck, carried by her owner Meghan Abrego, took the stage. After Olivia nipped at the microphone several times and let out a “quack quack quack,” Abrego translated for the duck.

“What was that?” Abrego said. “Landslide win?”

The Initiative, which had been the subject of much online discourse, passed 73% to 23%, with over 97,000 voting in favor of the initiative.

The effort had earned high-profile supporters in the lead-up to the vote, including mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George. But it also had its detractors in the form of some prominent D.C. chefs and restaurateurs.

Celebrity chef José Andrés, who has a foie gras dish on the menu of one of his many D.C.-area restaurants, pushed back strongly against the ban in social media posts, suggesting that there are more pressing societal issues to be focused on and questioning the merits of singling out foie gras as opposed to “banning all meats.” Bart Hutchins, chef at Butterworth’s in Capitol Hill, similarly compared the production of foie gras to commercial farming practices that he described as more harmful to animals.

Other chefs, like Geoff Tracy, the owner of Chef Geoff’s, opposed the ban on the grounds that restaurants, already on shaky ground due to the city’s economic slump, should be able to make their own decisions of what they serve. “It’s one additional regulation or one more thing we have to deal with,” Tracy told The Washington Sun last month. “Just leave us alone for a little bit.”

The word of Andrés, in particular, seemed to carry some weight. Ward 3 voter Robert Rosamelia said that while he understood the concerns about the farming practice, he had been moved by Andrés' stand against the ban.

“It feels like something chefs should be able to talk to their patrons about,” Rosamelia told The Sun after casting his ballot Tuesday.

Others went into the voting booth without much of an opinion. “It just was not a priority topic,” said Ward 4 resident Beth Washington, who voted against the ban. “I think there's other, more important things that I would vote on or be concerned about voting about.”

But the vivid language on the ballot, describing the practice as the “force-feeding of birds to enlarge their livers,” proved persuasive for some.

“We didn’t know a lot about it, but we didn’t like force-feeding poor ducks, so we voted for the initiative," said Ward 3 voter Joanne Howes.

The ban on the sale of foie gras is expected to go into effect July 1 of next year.
